name: Drafting Statements and Disclosures
title: Drafting Statements and Disclosures
answer: Drafting statements and disclosures covers the preparation of financial statements, the notes that accompany them, management discussion and analysis, and regulatory filings such as annual reports and quarterly updates. It includes both the numbers that come from the ledger and the narrative that explains them, along with the cross references that tie the two together. The work sits inside financial reporting and synthesis, where accounting policy, transaction data, and disclosure requirements meet. It also touches earnings releases, proxy statements, and sustainability or climate disclosures when those are part of the reporting package.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the financial close and consolidation stack, including the general ledger, subledgers, consolidation tools, and a controlled document repository. AI components typically sit alongside that stack, using large language models and retrieval augmented generation over accounting standards, internal accounting policy manuals, prior period filings, and disclosure checklists. Data pipelines move trial balances, journal entries, and supporting schedules into a structured layer, often with XBRL taxonomies for tagging. Access controls, version history, and a full audit trail are part of the infrastructure because the output is a regulated document.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts with a human setting the reporting calendar, materiality thresholds, and the list of required disclosures. The AI then drafts narrative sections by retrieving relevant guidance and prior language, while reconciliation checks tie every figure back to the trial balance or a supporting schedule. Accountants and legal reviewers edit the draft, resolve inconsistencies, and confirm that the disclosure is complete and accurate. The final version is locked, tagged, and routed through disclosure controls before filing.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk, and provenance are central because a misstatement can carry regulatory and legal consequences. Each AI generated sentence needs a traceable source, whether that is a ledger account, a contract, an accounting standard, or a prior filing, and the system should record who or what produced it and when. Confidential and material nonpublic information must stay within approved environments, with permissions that match the user's role. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect how much of this work sits under supervisory expectations, and human review remains the control that catches hallucination, stale language, or an unsupported claim.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more continuous reporting, deeper XBRL and inline XBRL tagging, and AI assistance that drafts and checks disclosures in near real time. Regulators and auditors are likely to ask for evidence about how an AI assisted draft was produced, reviewed, and approved. Tighter integration between the ledger, the disclosure management system, and the audit trail is likely, so that narrative and numbers stay linked from source to filing. The human role shifts toward judgment, exception handling, and sign off rather than manual assembly.
